sites.name: 1905 Mine
sites.location: Hurricane Hill / Boulder County Tungsten Mining District
overview: The 1905 Mine was a small but documented tungsten producer beside Hurricane Hill Road in the Boulder County tungsten district.
USGS records place the mine 825 feet south 25 degrees west of the Vasco No. 1 shaft and describe shaft workings associated with a ferberite-bearing vein along the Hurricane Hill breccia reef.

timeline.text: USGS indicates the mine may have produced tungsten before the surviving detailed production records begin.
The mine was productive during the World War I tungsten boom. Incomplete USGS records document about 250 units of WO3 from ore averaging 12.9 percent WO3.
USGS reported no known later production and estimated that total historic output may have exceeded 1,000 units of WO3.

moreHistory: U.S. Geological Survey Professional Paper 245 describes the 1905 Mine at roughly 8,550 feet elevation beside Hurricane Hill Road. The documented position is relative to the Vasco No. 1 shaft, which provides a defensible historic mine-level Scan anchor while avoiding a claim that the exact shaft collar has been surveyed by Remnant.

The mine was developed by shaft workings that USGS believed were probably no more than about 150 feet deep. The vein lies in the hanging wall of the Hurricane Hill breccia reef, striking roughly northeast and dipping northwest through aplite and granite.

USGS attributes the property to Gold, Silver, & Tungsten, Inc. during the documented production period. The retained production figures are incomplete, so Remnant presents them as reported historical estimates rather than precise lifetime totals.

sites.name: Afterthought Mine
overview: The Afterthought Mine is a documented Jamestown Mining District fluorspar locality west of Jamestown with a stable mapped mine/tunnel anchor.
Federal mineral records preserve the site as a fluorite occurrence and modern USGS-derived mapping places the mine at approximately 40.12221, -105.40055.

timeline.text: The Afterthought workings were developed as part of the Jamestown district's fluorspar and metal-mining landscape.
Federal Jamestown-district mineral mapping retained the Afterthought Mine as a named fluorite locality.
USGS/GNIS-derived mapping preserves a stable mine-level point for identification, though Remnant does not claim that point is a field-surveyed portal collar.

moreHistory: USGS-linked mineral references identify the Afterthought Mine in Boulder County's Jamestown Mining District and record fluorite at the locality.

The mapped Afterthought Mine and Walker Tunnel share the same published mine-level coordinate, so Remnant treats the coordinate as a defensible locality anchor rather than asserting a specific surviving opening without field confirmation.
No defensible site-specific photograph with clear app-use rights was found in the media search; unrelated Jamestown mine photographs were rejected rather than attached to the wrong location.

sites.name: Alamakee

moreHistory: USGS mining history documents the Alamakee name at Gold Hill, while mapped locality evidence provides a stable mine-level identification anchor near 40.06611, -105.40472.
The known 1895 archival photograph is retained as research evidence, but its item-level reuse basis is not sufficiently clear for Remnant packaging. It is therefore not shipped in the app.

sites.name: Alaska Tunnel

moreHistory: The mapped locality near 40.07333, -105.50667 provides a defensible historic tunnel-level Scan anchor without claiming that Remnant has field-surveyed a surviving portal opening.
A focused exact-site media search did not verify a publishable Alaska Tunnel photograph; nearby Ward-district imagery was rejected rather than assigned to the wrong tunnel.

sites.name: Alpine Horn

timeline.text: Archival records preserve a lawsuit filed by Alpine Horn owner J. N. Esselstyn against the United States Gold Corporation, reflecting active property interests in the Sugarloaf mining landscape.
Boulder County Parks and Open Space purchased the Alpine Horn lode on the southeast side of Sugarloaf Mountain.

moreHistory: The Carnegie Library for Local History preserves an Alpine Horn collection containing mine documents, maps of the Alpine Horn workings, and plats of nearby mining properties.
Historic mapping continues to identify Alpine Horn Mine in the Sugarloaf area, supporting the documented mine locality near 40.027486, -105.411661.

overview: The Dorothy and Katie mines were important historic tungsten workings in Millionaire Gulch within the Boulder County tungsten district. Federal mining records document the two properties as closely related workings with substantial early twentieth-century activity.

timeline.text: Extensive development took place at the Dorothy and Katie mines during the World War I tungsten period.

Dorothy was worked again through the mid-1940s, while records also note limited later work at Katie, including activity in 1942.

sites.name: Acme Mine
overview: The Acme Mine was a major Louisville-area coal mine that operated from the late nineteenth century into 1928 and helped shape the town's industrial landscape.
Historic state and local records document deep shaft workings, company housing, railroad service, and repeated subsidence effects beneath Louisville.

timeline.text: The Acme Mine entered operation in Louisville during the expansion of Boulder County's northern coal field.
Colorado's coal-mine inspector described the Acme as a two-shaft mine about 190 feet deep, connected to the Colorado & Southern Railroad.
Rocky Mountain Fuel Company acquired the Acme and operated it through its final years.
Industrial Commission records document 81 Acme employees in a wage case involving Rocky Mountain Fuel Company.
The Acme Mine closed after decades of coal production beneath and around Louisville.

moreHistory: Colorado mine-inspector records describe a main shaft and air shaft serving a roughly six-foot coal seam, with the main shaft divided for hoisting, pipe lines, and emergency access.
Local historical records preserve 1911 photographs of the Rocky Mountain Fuel Company's Acme Mine and company houses, confirming the mine's substantial surface plant and community setting.
Historic Louisville research also documents subsidence associated with Acme workings beneath the town, showing how the mine's underground footprint affected the later urban landscape.

For Remnant identification, the USGS/GNIS mine point at approximately 39.98193, -105.13665 is used as the documented mine-level anchor rather than claiming a surviving shaft collar has been field-surveyed.

timeline.text: Boulder County's retained Harney-Lastoka historical research identifies the Ajax coal mine as established in 1890.
The mine formed part of the Louisville-area coal landscape that shaped local settlement and employment.

moreHistory: A mapped mine point at approximately 39.977763, -105.136652 is retained as a defensible historic mine-level Scan anchor. Remnant does not represent that point as a field-surveyed surviving shaft collar.
A focused media search did not locate a reusable exact-site Ajax photograph; similarly named Ajax mines elsewhere in Colorado were rejected as wrong-site material.

sites.name: Albion Mine

overview: Albion Mine is a documented historic mine locality near Lake Albion in Boulder County's Snowy Range Mining District.

Historic Boulder County sources place Camp Albion at the center of the Snowy Range district, while retained mineral-locality mapping provides a defensible mine-level identification point for Albion without claiming that a surviving opening has been field-surveyed.

timeline.text: The Snowy Range Mining District was organized during Boulder County's early mining period; later sources also called it the Albion Mining District after the nearby camp.
A Denver Public Library mining-place index records the Albion Mine as established by 1864.
Camp Albion developed as a small mining center near timberline and became the focal settlement of the Snowy Range district.

moreHistory: Boulder historical collections describe Camp Albion as a small western Boulder County mining center associated with the Snowy Range Mining District and preserve photographs of the camp and its ore-milling landscape.

A mapped Albion mineral locality at approximately 40.05000, -105.58528 is retained as the Basic Scan anchor. Remnant treats this as a defensible historic mine-level locality point, not as a claim that an open shaft, adit, or exact surviving collar has been field-verified.

Known archival Camp Albion photographs document the surrounding mining settlement rather than the exact Albion Mine component, and their item-level reuse terms do not provide a sufficiently clear basis for packaging them as the mine's app image.

sites.name: Caribou Ghost Town
overview: Caribou is a high-elevation ghost town northwest of Nederland that grew beside one of Boulder County's best-known nineteenth-century silver districts.

The settlement developed rapidly after rich silver discoveries on Caribou Hill in 1869, and surviving historical records document a substantial mining community shaped by repeated fires, epidemics, and the collapse of silver mining in the 1890s.

timeline.text: Prospectors identified rich silver-bearing veins on Caribou Hill, including the Caribou and Poorman lodes, triggering rapid development of the district.
A town had formed at Caribou; a federal mining history reported about 30 houses and 125 voters by November.
A major fire swept through Caribou, one of several disasters that damaged the settlement during its mining years.
The silver-price collapse and financial panic forced most mines in the district to close, accelerating Caribou's decline.
Another major fire struck the town, further reducing the surviving building stock.

moreHistory: U.S. Geological Survey histories describe the Grand Island-Caribou area as a silver district west of Boulder and northwest of Nederland. By the end of 1871, most of the richest lodes had been located and production had expanded rapidly.

Late-1870s photographs preserved by the Carnegie Library for Local History show Caribou as a developed mountain settlement. The archive identifies the Sherman House in one view and notes additional views by William Henry Jackson.
Caribou Ghost Town is distinct from the nearby Caribou Mine, Caribou Ranch, and later recording-studio history. The townsite is represented separately as the historic settlement itself.

sites.name: Denver, Boulder & Western Railway / Switzerland Trail of America
overview: The Switzerland Trail follows portions of a historic narrow-gauge railroad corridor that served Boulder County mining communities and later became a well-known scenic excursion route.

timeline.text: Early narrow-gauge construction linked Boulder County mining districts, and the route expanded through the mountain communities west of Boulder.
The Colorado and Northwestern promoted the mountain railroad as the Switzerland Trail of America to attract excursion traffic as well as mining-related business.
Rail service ended and the tracks were removed, leaving substantial portions of the former railroad grade in the landscape.
The Denver, Boulder and Western Railway Historic District, also known as the Switzerland Trail of America, was listed in the National Register of Historic Places.

moreHistory: The corridor was used by several narrow-gauge railroad companies, including the Greeley, Salt Lake and Pacific Railway, Colorado and Northwestern Railroad, and Denver, Boulder and Western Railroad. It carried ore, supplies, residents, and tourists through Boulder County's mountain mining country.

Boulder County continues to recognize the Switzerland Trail railroad line as an important part of the county's mining and transportation history. Portions of the historic roadbed remain visible and are used for modern recreation.

sites.name: Conger Mine
sites.location: Sherwood Creek / west of Mud Lake near Nederland
overview: The Conger Mine was the leading tungsten mine of the Boulder County tungsten district near Nederland, developed after Samuel Conger and J. H. Wanamaker recognized valuable ferberite ore around 1900.

Federal mining records describe a 991-foot shaft and an extensive underground system, while modern Boulder County restoration work still identifies the historic mine site along Sherwood Creek west of Mud Lake.

timeline.text: Conger and Wanamaker recovered about 40 tons of high-grade tungsten ore from leased ground near Nederland, and Conger identified the vein that became the district's most productive.
After the original lease ended, the property was expanded into a major tungsten operation as demand for tungsten steel increased.
The mine grew into one of the most important producers in the district during the tungsten boom associated with high-speed steel and World War I demand.
USGS estimates indicate that the Conger Mine supplied roughly 20 to 25 percent of the Boulder County district's historic tungsten output.
Boulder County and Colorado reclamation agencies advanced work along Sherwood Creek to address mine waste and restore the stream corridor at the historic Conger site.

moreHistory: U.S. Geological Survey Professional Paper 245 describes the Conger as the most productive vein in the Boulder County tungsten district and documents the scale of the underground workings. The mine became a centerpiece of the Nederland-area tungsten industry that expanded rapidly after 1900.

The same federal history places the discovery in the period when tungsten steel was becoming important for high-speed cutting tools. Prices and demand rose sharply through the early twentieth century, culminating in the World War I boom.

The mine's legacy remains visible in the landscape. Boulder County identifies the Conger Mine site along Sherwood Creek, west of Mud Lake, where recent reclamation work has focused on mine waste and restoration of the creek corridor.

sites.name: Blue Jay Mine
overview: Blue Jay Mine is a historic fluorspar mine southeast of Jamestown in Boulder County, where federal mining studies documented a substantial underground operation and Boulder County later preserved the site as a designated historic property.

timeline.text: Federal investigators described the Blue Jay Mine as developed by several short adits, a roughly 300-foot vertical shaft, and drifts on the 150- and 300-foot levels.
Federal teams sampled and examined the mine's lower workings during investigations of uranium-bearing minerals associated with the fluorite vein.
Boulder County designated Blue Jay Mine as a historic site, recognizing the surviving mining complex near Jamestown.

moreHistory: The Blue Jay vein was described by U.S. Geological Survey investigators as a northwest-trending structure more than 1,000 feet long, containing deep-purple crystalline fluorite with quartz, clay minerals, pyrite, galena, and uranium-bearing minerals.

Boulder County has described Blue Jay as one of the better-preserved and historically interesting mining complexes on its open-space properties. The surviving hoist-house area has also become important bat habitat, giving the historic mine an additional modern conservation role.

sites.name: Blue Goose Mine
overview: Blue Goose Mine is a documented inactive coal mine in Boulder County's Boulder-Weld coalfield and is preserved as a named mine feature on Louisville-area topographic mapping.
Published Colorado coal-mine mapping places Blue Goose among the historic underground coal workings in the Louisville and Marshall-area mining landscape.
moreHistory: USGS-derived mapping places the named mine at approximately 39.979985, -105.189432. The mapped mine locality is used to identify the historic site; no claim is made that a particular surviving shaft or underground opening has been field-verified or is accessible today.
A focused exact-site media search did not locate a defensible reusable historic photograph, so unrelated coal-mine imagery was not attached.

sites.name: Annie L.
sites.location: Boulder County Tungsten District, near Roosevelt Tunnel
overview: Annie L. is a documented historic tungsten mine in Boulder County's tungsten district, closely associated with the Roosevelt workings.
Colorado and federal mining records describe a 120-foot shaft with two levels and record substantial historic tungsten production from the property.

timeline.text: The Annie L./Roosevelt property saw its chief early production during the World War I tungsten boom.
Thayer and McClellan worked the Annie L. during renewed wartime tungsten activity.

moreHistory: Colorado Geological Survey records place Annie L. in SE1/4 Sec. 36, T1N R72W, about 900 feet S67°W of the Roosevelt tunnel. U.S. Geological Survey Professional Paper 245 likewise describes the Annie L. shaft about 900 feet west-southwest of Roosevelt and notes two eastward levels from the shaft.

The coordinates used here are an approximate mapped location calculated from the documented offset from the Roosevelt tunnel. No claim is made that a surviving open shaft, portal, or safe public access exists today.

sites.name: Black Rover Mine
overview: Black Rover Mine is a documented historic tungsten mine in Boulder County's tungsten district.
Colorado Geological Survey records describe an upper shaft and a lower adit and report more than 10,000 units of historic tungsten production, much of it produced between 1916 and 1931.

timeline.text: Most of the mine's documented tungsten production came from the upper shaft workings during this period.

moreHistory: Colorado Geological Survey MI-04 places Black Rover in SW1/4 Sec. 20, T1S R72W, about one-half mile southeast of the Mammoth shaft. It describes separate upper-shaft and lower-adit workings and cites U.S. Geological Survey Professional Paper 245, plate 7, as a map source.

USGS-derived topographic mapping preserves Black Rover Mine near 39.941654, -105.487497. This mapped historic mine locality is used here without claiming that any opening remains accessible or safe today.

sites.name: Barker No. 1 Mine
sites.location: Boulder County Tungsten District / Clark Tunnel
overview: Barker No. 1 was a historic tungsten mine developed from the Clark Tunnel in the Boulder County Tungsten District.
Colorado's 1960 tungsten-mine inventory places the Barker No. 1 workings about 200 feet inside the Clark Tunnel and records two working levels with historic tungsten production.
moreHistory: The state mine inventory estimates Barker No. 1 production at roughly 2,000 to 3,000 tungsten units and describes ore stopes above and below the Clark Tunnel level. U.S. Geological Survey work also describes the Barker No. 1 vein as a continuation of the Vasco No. 8 vein.

The coordinate used here is a documented Barker Mine / Clark Tunnel locality-level anchor near 39.97027, -105.48083. It identifies the historic mine area without claiming that Remnant has field-surveyed a surviving portal, shaft collar, or underground working.
A focused exact-site media search did not locate a defensible reusable Barker No. 1 image, so nearby tungsten-district photographs were rejected rather than attached to the wrong mine.

sites.name: Black Diamond Mine
sites.location: Lafayette / Baseline Road and U.S. 287 area
overview: Black Diamond Mine was a documented coal mine in the Lafayette area of Boulder County and part of the Boulder-Weld coal field.
Local historical records preserve the mine in Lafayette's twentieth-century coal-mining story, while USGS-derived mapping provides a stable mine-level location for identification.

timeline.text: A Lafayette historical photograph documents the interior of the Black Diamond Mine during its operating era.
Local and county historical sources identify Black Diamond as Lafayette's last coal mine to close.

moreHistory: USGS-derived mapping places the named Black Diamond Mine near 39.948597, -105.233878 and records it as an inactive coal mine; the mapped point is used as a mine-level identification location rather than a claim that a surviving shaft or opening has been field-surveyed.
A surviving 1942 photograph is retained as historical evidence, but its item-level reuse terms are not sufficiently clear for app use, so no image is included with this record.

sites.name: Iowa Mine
sites.location: Gordon Gulch / Boulder County Tungsten District
overview: Iowa Mine is a documented historic tungsten mine and short-adit working in Gordon Gulch in Boulder County's tungsten district.
Colorado's tungsten inventory records about 100 units of production from the property, with ferberite and scheelite in a granite-hosted vein.

timeline.text: Colorado Geological Survey records limited development by underhand stoping that produced fair-grade tungsten ore.

moreHistory: Colorado Geological Survey places Iowa in the northeast quarter of Section 34, T1N R72W, east of the Ophir-Miser group in Gordon Gulch, and describes the working as a short adit.
The retained coordinate represents the Gordon Gulch locality for identification and is not presented as a field-surveyed adit portal.

sites.name: Lower Rambler Mine
sites.location: Boulder County Tungsten District / SW1/4 Sec. 24, T1S R73W
overview: Lower Rambler Mine is a documented tungsten mine in Boulder County's tungsten district, west of the historic Tungsten shaft area.
Federal and Colorado mining records describe a deep Lower Rambler shaft and ferberite-bearing workings that produced tungsten during the twentieth century.

timeline.text: USGS records state that the Lower Rambler shaft was sunk during the 1930s.
Small production was reported from level workings driven by Tom Walsh, with the Cowdery brothers identified as owners at the time.
Colorado's tungsten-mine inventory records the main shaft at about 200 feet deep and notes additional drifting and crosscutting under a federal exploration contract.

moreHistory: USGS Professional Paper 245 places Lower Rambler at about 8,590 feet elevation, roughly 1,800 feet west-northwest of the Tungsten shaft, and documents ferberite-bearing feeder veins in the mine workings.

The Colorado tungsten inventory places the Rambler-Lower Rambler property in the southwest quarter of Section 24, Township 1 South, Range 73 West and distinguishes the Lower Rambler main shaft from the shallower Rambler workings.

The retained coordinate is a conservative mine-group locality associated with the documented Rambler-Lower Rambler occurrence; it is not represented as a field-surveyed surviving shaft collar or an access point.

sites.name: Illinois Mine
sites.location: Northwest of Nederland / Boulder County Tungsten District
overview: Illinois Mine was a documented tungsten mine northwest of Nederland and one of the principal properties operated by the Wolf Tongue Mining Company in the Boulder County tungsten district.

timeline.text: Wolf Tongue Mining Company operated the Illinois Mine as one of its principal tungsten properties near Nederland.
U.S. Geological Survey Professional Paper 245 documented the Illinois workings and their place within the Boulder County tungsten district.

moreHistory: State and federal mining records place the Illinois Mine roughly northwest of Nederland and document substantial underground workings, including a deep shaft and multiple levels.
The mine formed part of the tungsten-producing landscape around Nederland that became nationally important during the first half of the twentieth century.

sites.name: Kekionga Mine
sites.location: Upper Magnolia Road / Magnolia Mining District
overview: Kekionga Mine is a documented historic Boulder County mine above Magnolia, where Colorado Geological Survey records describe tungsten workings reached by the upper Magnolia road.

timeline.text: Colorado Geological Survey records the Kekionga property with a shaft more than 200 feet deep, additional shafts and cuts, and production of about 2,000 tungsten units.
The same state record notes that the last work was carried out under an RFC loan and that combined gold-and-tungsten ore was developed.

moreHistory: Colorado Geological Survey MI-04 places the workings on the south line of Section 6, Township 1 South, Range 71 West, above Magnolia, and notes that the upper Magnolia road passes between the mine dumps.
USGS-derived place mapping retains the Kekionga Mine locality at approximately 39.9858196, -105.3841605, consistent with the documented Magnolia-area mine setting.

sites.name: Barker No. 3
sites.location: Boulder County Tungsten Mining District / Clark Tunnel area
overview: Barker No. 3 was a documented tungsten mine in Boulder County's historic tungsten district, developed through two surface shafts, adits, and a lower connection reached from the Clark Tunnel.

Colorado and U.S. Geological Survey records identify the property in the northeast quarter of Section 18, T1S R72W, and report production of at least about 6,000 units of tungsten concentrate during the district's active mining era.

timeline.text: Barker No. 3 was developed as part of the dense network of tungsten workings west of the former Tungsten settlement in Boulder County.
State and federal mine reports documented two upper shafts, an adit entering southwest of the shaft area, another caved adit, and a separate Clark Tunnel section with a drift and winze.
Colorado's Metal Mining Fund summarized Barker No. 3 as a former producer with recorded output of 6,000 tungsten units or more and cited USGS Professional Paper 245 as the principal mapped source.

moreHistory: Colorado's Tungsten Mines of Colorado places Barker No. 3 in NE1/4 Section 18, T1S R72W. It locates the shaft 1,175 feet southwest of the Vasco No. 6 shaft and records the Barker vein about 650 feet inside the Clark Tunnel.

The same state report describes two distinct working sections. The upper section included two shafts, an adit entering from southwest of the shaft, and another adit that was already caved when documented. The lower Clark Tunnel section consisted of about 110 feet of drift on the vein and a 25-foot winze.

USGS Professional Paper 245 includes a plan of the Barker No. 3 workings and geologic surface sketch. Remnant uses an approximate historic mine-level identification point derived from the documented Barker No. 3/Vasco No. 6 spatial relationship; it does not claim that an individual shaft collar or surviving opening has been field-surveyed or is safe or accessible today.

sites.name: Boulder Valley Mine
overview: The Boulder Valley Mine was one of the defining coal mines of early Erie and, for a time, became Colorado's largest coal producer as railroad access expanded the Northern Coalfield.
The historic mine site lies near today's Coal Creek Disc Golf Course and the old Boulder Valley rail corridor, where the former workings helped shape Erie's growth as a coal town.

timeline.text: The Boulder Valley Railroad reached Erie, stimulating renewed development of the Northern Coalfield and a surge in production from the Boulder Valley Mine.
A miners' strike at the Boulder Valley Mine escalated during the episode remembered locally as the Erie War, and troops were brought in to maintain order.
Miners again struck for improved working conditions. The operating company removed machinery and abandoned the works after the strike continued.
The Boulder Valley Mine reopened under new ownership and remained part of Erie's coal-mining landscape.

moreHistory: Town of Erie historical material identifies the Boulder Valley Mine as a major early producer in the Northern Coalfield and links the mine directly to Erie's development as an important Colorado coal town.

Modern local interpretation places the original mine beside the historic railroad alignment near the Coal Creek Disc Golf Course. A USGS-derived mapped mine point at approximately 40.049429, -105.042481 provides a defensible mine-level identification anchor; Remnant does not represent that point as a field-surveyed surviving shaft collar.

Contemporary reporting and local interpretation note that the former entrance has been filled and mine structures no longer survive, while portions of the historic mining landscape remain visible near the route.

sites.name: Bed Dig Mine
sites.location: About one mile northwest of Nederland / Boulder County Tungsten Mining District
overview: Bed Dig Mine, spelled Beddig Mine in federal records, was one of the more productive tungsten mines of the Boulder County tungsten district about a mile northwest of Nederland.
U.S. Geological Survey reporting places the mine just west of the Conger Mine and documents sustained early-twentieth-century development on the Crow patent.

timeline.text: Colorado Tungsten Corporation worked the mine intensively and developed it to the fifth level.
Primos Chemical Company operated the Beddig in conjunction with the adjoining Conger Mine.
Sublessees carried out limited additional work while the Crow patent was leased by Wolf Tongue Mining Company, but production during this period was small.

moreHistory: U.S. Geological Survey Professional Paper 245 states that the Beddig ranked among the district's leading mines by total output and describes the property as part of the Crow patent, owned by Colorado Tungsten Corporation from 1905.
The same federal study documents the mine's underground development and its close operational relationship with the neighboring Conger Mine during the World War I tungsten boom.
Modern USGS-derived topographic place data preserves the Beddig Mine as a named inactive tungsten mine on the Nederland quadrangle at approximately 39.982209, -105.527221.
